pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 12–14 (centrality 0.228, a hub node). The 'Big Five' mass extinctions — End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, K-Pg — their differing kill mechanisms, and the crucial idea that extinction also OPENS ecological space for later radiations — taught by comparing events and tracing cause→effect→recovery.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS3 biology (extinction; how organisms affect and are affected by environments) and Earth science (Earth's history); working-scientifically comparing evidence across cases.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS4-1 (fossil record documents existence, diversity, extinction and change) and MS-ESS2/ESS1 (Earth systems and history).
• Operational details: place the five events on the geologic timeline with approximate dates; attach a kill mechanism to each — End-Ordovician (glaciation/sea-level fall), Late Devonian (ocean anoxia), End-Permian ('the Great Dying', ~252 Mya, most severe, Siberian Traps mega-volcanism → warming, acidification, anoxia), End-Triassic (volcanism/CAMP), K-Pg (asteroid impact). Then the recovery half: each extinction was followed by an adaptive RADIATION into vacated niches — K-Pg removing non-avian dinosaurs let mammals diversify, ultimately to humans.
• Checkpoint: Tier A: name the Big Five in order and roughly when. Tier B: match each event to its main kill mechanism, and identify the most severe (End-Permian). Tier C: explain the extinction→radiation logic using the K-Pg→mammals example.
bestPractices: Teach comparatively — line the five events up so students contrast severity and mechanism rather than memorising them in isolation.
Pair every extinction with its recovery/radiation, so the concept is understood as reset-and-rediversify, not just death.
Anchor severity visually (End-Permian ~90% loss deepest) to correct the assumption that K-Pg was the biggest.
Distinguish background extinction from mass extinction (large fraction of species, short time, global driver).
Use the K-Pg→mammals→humans chain to make the extinction→radiation idea personally meaningful.
keyRepresentations: A biodiversity-through-time curve with five marked dips.
A geologic timeline labelling each event's date.
A niche-vacancy→radiation diagram (e.g. mammals filling post-dinosaur niches).
A severity bar comparing % species lost across the Big Five.
commonMisconceptions: 'The K-Pg (dinosaur) extinction was the biggest' — the End-Permian was far more severe.
'All mass extinctions had the same cause (asteroids)' — mechanisms differ (glaciation, anoxia, volcanism, impact).
'Extinction is purely destructive' — it also opens niches enabling adaptive radiations.
'Mass extinctions happen instantly' — some unfolded over thousands to hundreds of thousands of years.
'Species that survived were the strongest/most advanced' — survival often reflected small size, generalism or luck, not superiority.

learn.summary: For ages 12–14: compare the 'Big Five' mass extinctions (End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic, K-Pg), attach each to its main proposed kill mechanism (noting that some mechanisms, such as volcanism and ocean anoxia, appear in more than one event), rank the End-Permian as most severe, and — crucially — understand each extinction as reset-and-rediversify: catastrophe clears ecological space that later enables adaptive radiations (e.g. mammals after the K-Pg, a lineage that eventually included humans). Learners place events on a geologic timeline, trace cause→collapse→recovery, and correct the assumption that the famous K-Pg was the biggest.

activities.title: Run the crash and the recovery on a biodiversity timeline
feedback: If a learner ranks K-Pg as most severe, show the severity comparison: End-Permian ~90% species lost is deeper than the K-Pg toll — fame is not severity.
If a learner treats all extinctions as asteroid-caused, revisit each mechanism separately (glaciation, anoxia, volcanism, impact) so the differences stand out.
If a learner sees only destruction, direct them to the recovery phase: emptied niches let survivors diversify, as mammals did after the K-Pg.
If a learner thinks extinctions are instant, note that some unfolded over thousands to hundreds of thousands of years, and the Late Devonian over millions of years in several pulses.
activities.rationale: The objective is comparative and causal, so lining events up and tracing cause→collapse→recovery makes the reset-and-rediversify logic concrete rather than a memorised list. Live mechanism/recovery controls and a side-by-side compare-mode are optional supports that may make the mechanism more visible; the same comparison can be traced on an annotated static curve. The cited sources are attached as support for the factual content of this insight (the Big Five, End-Permian severity, K-Pg→mammal radiation); they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular medium.
sourceClaims: Earth has had five major ('Big Five') mass extinctions — End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic and End-Cretaceous (K-Pg) — each removing a large fraction of species in a geologically short time.

The End-Permian extinction (~252 Mya) was the most severe ('the Great Dying'), associated with the Siberian Traps volcanism and consequent warming, ocean acidification and anoxia; the K-Pg extinction removed non-avian dinosaurs and was followed by the adaptive radiation of mammals.
learnerActions: Work with a biodiversity-through-time curve stretched across the geologic timeline, with the five Big Five events marked as dips.

Select an event and link it to its own kill mechanism: End-Ordovician (glaciation and sea-level fall), Late Devonian (ocean anoxia), End-Permian (Siberian Traps mega-volcanism → warming, acidification, anoxia, ~252 Mya), End-Triassic (volcanism/CAMP), K-Pg (asteroid impact).
If a dynamic model is available, trigger each mechanism and watch the diversity curve drop — deepest at the End-Permian (~90% of species) — so severity is seen, not just asserted.

For each event, move to a 'recovery' phase and watch or trace surviving groups radiate into emptied niches; after the K-Pg, follow small mammals fanning out into the niches non-avian dinosaurs left, a radiation that over tens of millions of years produced a lineage eventually including humans — a plausible consequence of the clearing, not a guaranteed one.
Use a compare-mode to overlay two events' severity and mechanism side by side and state which was more severe and why.
Write one sentence capturing the two-sided idea: a mass extinction is both an ending and a reset that enables re-diversification.
activities.intendedInsight: Mass extinctions differ in cause and severity; each catastrophe both removes a large fraction of species and opens ecological space, so extinction and the later adaptive radiation, which typically took millions of years to unfold, are linked parts of the same reset-and-rediversify story.

activities.title: Annotated diversity curve: read each dip
feedback: If a learner cannot say what radiated after an event, prompt them to connect the empty niches to the group that later diversified (e.g. mammals after K-Pg).
If severity ranking is wrong, compare the depths of the dips directly on the graph.
activities.rationale: A fixed annotated graph does not let a learner trigger a mechanism or watch a radiation unfold, but it still teaches the comparison clearly and supports reading severity and sequence. It works well as a companion or when interactive models are unavailable; this is an affordance/limit statement, not a claim that one medium is superior. The cited claims support the factual content read from the curve.
sourceClaims: Earth has had five major ('Big Five') mass extinctions — End-Ordovician, Late Devonian, End-Permian, End-Triassic and End-Cretaceous (K-Pg) — each removing a large fraction of species in a geologically short time.

The End-Permian extinction (~252 Mya) was the most severe ('the Great Dying'), associated with the Siberian Traps volcanism and consequent warming, ocean acidification and anoxia; the K-Pg extinction removed non-avian dinosaurs and was followed by the adaptive radiation of mammals.
learnerActions: Examine a single annotated diversity-through-time graph with the five dips marked.
For each dip, identify its date, approximate severity (% species lost), kill mechanism, and the radiation that followed.
Mark which dip is deepest and explain why the End-Permian is deepest despite the K-Pg being better known.
Explain in your own words what 'radiated afterward' means for at least one event.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear comparison of dates, severities, mechanisms and recoveries can be read directly from a well-labelled curve, reinforcing that the five events differ and each is followed by diversification.

activities.title: Sequence, match and explain (check understanding)
feedback: If matching errs toward one shared cause, re-separate the mechanisms.
If the K-Pg is ranked most severe, compare it to the End-Permian's ~90% loss.
Push for an explanation of WHY emptied niches enable radiation, not just naming the mammal example.
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching efficiently check the comparison, but the explanation step must be constructed by the learner so that the causal reset-and-rediversify idea is produced, not merely recognised. Recognition/matching items check classification but do not by themselves elicit an independent explanation.
sourceClaims: The End-Permian extinction (~252 Mya) was the most severe ('the Great Dying'), associated with the Siberian Traps volcanism and consequent warming, ocean acidification and anoxia; the K-Pg extinction removed non-avian dinosaurs and was followed by the adaptive radiation of mammals.
learnerActions: Order the Big Five chronologically with approximate dates.
Match each event to its main kill mechanism.
State which extinction was most severe (End-Permian) and justify the ranking.
Explain the extinction→radiation logic using the K-Pg→mammals→(eventually) humans chain in a written or spoken response, not just a selected option.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to sequence, match, rank severity and explain the extinction→radiation link demonstrates the full concept rather than isolated recall.

activities.title: Ask a palaeobiologist (perspective extension)
feedback: If a learner claims survivors were 'the fittest/most advanced', note that survival often reflected small size, generalism or chance, not superiority.
Redirect open discussion back to the evidence: what distinguishes a 'mass' extinction (large fraction of species, short time, global driver) from background extinction.
activities.rationale: Dialogue broadens perspective and motivation but does not itself build the comparative timeline, so it is positioned as an extension rather than the core activity.
learnerActions: Pose questions a palaeobiologist could discuss, e.g. 'Why did roughly 90% of species die in the Great Dying?' or 'Are we entering a sixth mass extinction?'
After discussing, relate the answer back to the comparative timeline: how does this event's cause and severity sit against the others?
Consider why survivors were often small, generalist or simply lucky rather than 'the strongest or most advanced'.
activities.intendedInsight: Expert discussion can add depth and real-world relevance (severity drivers, the possibility of a current sixth extinction, the role of luck in survival) that complements the core comparative-causal analysis.

constraints: Distinguish background extinction from mass extinction: a mass extinction removes a large fraction of species, in a geologically short time, under a global driver.
Make severity visible/explicit so learners do not assume the famous K-Pg was the biggest; the End-Permian (~90% loss) was deepest.
Keep each event tied to its own mechanism; do not generalise the asteroid cause to all five.
Always pair each extinction with its recovery/radiation so the concept is reset-and-rediversify, not death alone.
Note that some extinctions unfolded over thousands to hundreds of thousands of years, and the Late Devonian over millions of years in several pulses, rather than instantly.
Recognition/matching tasks check the comparison but do not by themselves show a learner can explain the extinction→radiation causal link; include a constructed explanation.
Present the mammals-after-K-Pg chain, including the eventual emergence of humans, as a plausible evolutionary consequence of cleared niches, not as a deterministic certainty.

Live mechanism levers, recovery animations and compare-mode overlays are optional aids that may make the mechanism more concrete; they are not required, and the same comparison can be taught on a static annotated curve.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; the two listed sources were not re-fetched and are marked verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The cited sources establish the factual content taught (the Big Five, End-Permian severity, K-Pg→mammal radiation); they do not establish that any interactive medium is necessary or more effective than another, so medium claims are kept as optional/'may' wording.
Approximate figures (~252 Mya for End-Permian, ~90% species loss) are carried from the source and pedagogy fields; treat as approximate and confirm against current references if used for assessment.

The 'owe our existence to the asteroid' framing is a motivational narrative; the K-Pg→mammals→humans chain is presented as a plausible evolutionary consequence that did occur, not a deterministic necessity.

The original row claimed a static image 'can't' let a child run a mechanism and that 3D 'would decorate rather than deepen'; these catalog-fit judgements have been softened to affordance/limit statements, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Kill mechanisms for several events (e.g. Late Devonian anoxia, End-Triassic CAMP volcanism) are areas of ongoing scientific discussion; the row presents single main mechanisms — present them as the leading proposed causes.

Only two coarse source claims are available; where activities 2–4 rely on the same facts they reuse those claims, and the sixth-extinction / survivor-luck points in the conversation extension have no directly supporting source claim (left as []) and should be treated as unverified.

probeDeeper: The Siberian Traps were enormous volcanic eruptions — how could volcanism on that scale cause a global extinction?
If the K-Pg extinction hadn't happened, why might large mammals — and humans — never have arisen?
Two mass extinctions had different causes but similar effects — what does that tell you about what makes an extinction 'mass'?
assess.correctAnswer: No — the End-Permian extinction (~252 million years ago), linked to the Siberian Traps volcanic eruptions, was far more severe, wiping out around 90% of species. And while catastrophic, mass extinctions also clear ecological space: after the K-Pg removed the non-avian dinosaurs, mammals radiated and diversified, eventually including us. Destruction and later diversification are two sides of the same event.

errorPatterns.pattern: The K-Pg was the biggest/most severe mass extinction because it's the most famous.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare severities — End-Permian ~90% of species versus K-Pg's lower toll; fame is not severity.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the K-Pg was the deadliest mass extinction in Earth's history.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Ranks K-Pg as the deadliest, unaware of the far larger End-Permian event.

errorPatterns.pattern: A mass extinction is only a catastrophe — nothing good for life can come from it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce adaptive radiation: emptied niches let surviving groups (e.g. mammals after K-Pg) diversify rapidly.
errorPatterns.distractor: A mass extinction is purely a disaster; nothing good comes after it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies any evolutionary consequence, seeing only destruction.

errorPatterns.pattern: All five mass extinctions had the same cause (an asteroid, like K-Pg).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish mechanisms — glaciation, oceanic anoxia, volcanic mega-eruptions, impact — across the five events.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Generalises the asteroid mechanism to every mass extinction.

responseLevels.gap: Assumes K-Pg was the most severe and sees mass extinction only as destruction, with no sense of differing causes.
responseLevels.full: Orders the five events, identifies the End-Permian (Siberian Traps) as most severe, distinguishes their kill mechanisms, and explains how extinctions open ecological space for subsequent radiations such as mammals after K-Pg.
responseLevels.partial: Names several mass extinctions or one adaptive radiation, but can't both rank the End-Permian as most severe AND link extinctions to later diversification.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: The K-Pg asteroid extinction that killed the non-avian dinosaurs is the most famous mass extinction. Was it the most severe one Earth has ever had? And is a mass extinction purely a disaster, or can it also do something for life afterwards? Explain.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who equates 'most famous' with 'most severe' names K-Pg as the biggest. A child who understands ranks the End-Permian as most severe AND grasps that extinctions open space for adaptive radiations.
